questions.enonce_markdown: A complex number $z$ satisfies the equation $\dfrac{z}{z+2} = 2 - i$. Express $z$ in the form $a + bi$, where $a$ and $b$ are real constants. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Multiply both sides by $z + 2$ (note $z \ne -2$):

$$z = (2 - i)(z + 2) = (2 - i)z + 2(2 - i).$$

Collect the terms in $z$:

$$z - (2 - i)z = 4 - 2i \;\Longrightarrow\; (-1 + i)z = 4 - 2i \;\Longrightarrow\; z = \frac{4 - 2i}{-1 + i}.$$

Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, $-1 - i$:

$$z = \frac{(4 - 2i)(-1 - i)}{(-1 + i)(-1 - i)} = \frac{-4 - 4i + 2i + 2i^2}{1 + 1} = \frac{-4 - 2i - 2}{2} = \frac{-6 - 2i}{2}.$$

$$\boxed{z = -3 - i}$$

Check: $z + 2 = -1 - i$ and $(2 - i)(-1 - i) = -2 - 2i + i + i^2 = -3 - i = z$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The vector equations of two lines are given by

$$\mathbf{r} = 3\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k} + \lambda(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}) \quad\text{and}\quad \mathbf{r} = 3\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k} + \mu(\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}).$$

Find the vector normal to the plane containing both lines. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The direction vectors are $\mathbf{d}_1 = 2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{d}_2 = \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$.

**The lines are coplanar.** Equate the two position vectors: $3 + 2\lambda = 3 + \mu$, $6 + 3\lambda = -1 - 2\mu$, $1 - \lambda = 4 + \mu$. From the first, $\mu = 2\lambda$; the second gives $6 + 3\lambda = -1 - 4\lambda$, so $\lambda = -1$ and $\mu = -2$; the third is satisfied ($1 + 1 = 2 = 4 - 2$). So the lines intersect at $(1, 3, 2)$ and therefore lie in a single plane.

**Normal vector.** A vector normal to the plane is perpendicular to both directions, so take their vector product:

$$\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2 = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \mathbf{i}(3 - 2) - \mathbf{j}(2 + 1) + \mathbf{k}(-4 - 3) = \mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} - 7\mathbf{k}.$$

$$\boxed{\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} - 7\mathbf{k}}$$

(any non-zero multiple of this vector is also normal). Check: $\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}_1 = 2 - 9 + 7 = 0$ and $\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}_2 = 1 + 6 - 7 = 0$.

questions.enonce_markdown: Obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane containing both lines. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The plane has normal $\mathbf{n} = (1, -3, -7)$ and passes through the point of intersection $(1, 3, 2)$ (or through $(3, 6, 1)$, the first line's base point). The equation is $\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}$:

$$x - 3y - 7z = (1)(1) - 3(3) - 7(2) = 1 - 9 - 14 = -22.$$

$$\boxed{x - 3y - 7z = -22 \quad (\text{i.e. } x - 3y - 7z + 22 = 0)}$$

Check with the base points of both lines: $(3, 6, 1)$: $3 - 18 - 7 = -22$; $(3, -1, 4)$: $3 + 3 - 28 = -22$. Both satisfy the equation, as does $(1, 3, 2)$.
